candidate.answerReason: Exactly five qualifying rolls contribute \(12/729\), and six qualifying rolls contribute \(1/729\), giving \(13/729\).

methods.label: Separate exactly five and exactly six
methods.explanation:
Call a roll successful when it shows \(5\) or \(6\). A success has probability \(2/6=1/3\), and a failure has probability \(2/3\). The six rolls are independent.

At least five successes means exactly five or exactly six. For exactly five, choose the position of the unique failure in \(6\) ways. For any fixed failure position, independence gives probability
\[
\left(\frac13\right)^5\frac23.
\]
These six cases do not overlap because the unique failure has only one position. Six successes have probability \((1/3)^6\).

The five-success and six-success cases are disjoint and exhaust the requested event, so its probability is
\[
6\left(\frac13\right)^5\frac23
+\left(\frac13\right)^6
=\frac{12+1}{729}
=\frac{13}{729}.
\]
The answer is \(\boxed{\text{A}}\).
methods.levelReason: Uses elementary independent-event multiplication and a direct count of the six possible failure positions.

candidate.annotationRationale: The task asks for a binomial success-count probability. The method derives the relevant probabilities from independent rolls and adds disjoint cases using cnm_h138. It does not require the binomial theorem or a general combinations formula.
